title: Chapter 27 – The Fortieth Step
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

Forty steps, and Lin Jian has counted them every time.

He counts them now, going down behind his grandfather's broad green back, with the Light Orb slip in the old man's left hand throwing a pale circle on the stone. The upper steps are cold. They are always cold, the cold of rock that has never once been touched by the sun. At the tenth step the air stops smelling of the stone hut and begins to smell of something older, wet iron and pine resin and something sweeter underneath that he has never managed to name. At the twentieth, the cold begins to loosen. At the thirtieth, he can feel it on the backs of his hands: a faint, steady warmth, like the flank of a sleeping animal.

Grandfather does not hurry. He has not hurried in a week. He moves down the stair in the deep-green Patriarch robe with the pine crest stitched at the breast, the plain old sword at his hip, and his right hand trailing along the wall as if he is greeting each stone by name. His breath makes no sound at all.

"Count aloud," he says.

"Thirty-one."

"Thirty-two is the one your father tripped on, at nine. He cried. I told him the stone had done it on purpose." The old man's voice is dry and unhurried. "Thirty-three."

"Thirty-three."

"The Compact will be read tomorrow. By then it will not matter what I tell you tonight, because you will already have decided what to think. So I will tell you now, while you are still a boy of nine and I am still a man with breath in him." He pauses on the thirty-fifth step. "Close your eyes."

Lin Jian closes them.

Beneath his boots, the stone hums. Not a sound; a knowing. The fragment sewn into his inner collar presses against his collarbone like a small warm coin, and a faint line of text brushes the edge of his sight and fades before he can read it. The vein is vast and slow. Something else lies under the vein, as a stone lies under a river.

"Open."

They are standing on the fortieth step.

It is not a step that anyone would look at twice. Three times already, in lamplight, he has stepped over it on his way into the chamber. Dark basalt, unworn, not a nick on its edge, as if no foot has ever crossed it. It is too dark to be called gray and too smooth to be called rough, and in the lamp's flat light it looks like what it looks like: a plain stone.

Grandfather lowers the Light Orb until its glow is a thumb of warm gold at the level of his knee. He turns the slip sideways. The light rakes across the step at a low angle, the way a farmer looks along a furrow.

Lin Jian forgets to breathe.

The step is covered in lines.

Fine as the veins of a leaf, thousands of them, running in every direction, curling back on themselves, branching and rejoining and thinning to nothing. They are not carved. They are not painted. They lie in the stone itself, a pale, shallow tracery that appears only when the light is almost level. They are not quite a spiral and not quite a web, and as his eye follows one it slips onto another, and then another, and he has the dizzying sense of looking at a map of a country that has no edges.

In the middle of the lines, pressed deep into the basalt, is a hand.

It is a man's right hand, broad, with the fingers a little spread. The print is not worn but finished, each whorl of the fingertips distinct, the way a seal's face is distinct after it has been set in wax. The lines flow into it, around it, away from it. Whoever put his palm to this stone put it there to ask something, and the stone answered.

"My grandfather," says Lin Zhenshan. "Lin Shoucheng. The first of us to hold this hill."

Two percent. He holds the number in his mind without letting his face move. It is a tiny number. But he has seen the fragment's own lines, the pale tracery under his collar, and he knows what a match looks like at ninety percent and at fifty and at ten. Two percent is not coincidence. Two percent is a signature on the same hand.

Level four. It is the first time the panel has ever shown him a rung he cannot see. He tucks it away to think about later, next to a hundred other things he has tucked away.

"I was nine," says Grandfather, "when he told me. The night before he died. I was sitting on the end of his bed, being very proud of myself because I had learned the second form of the Lin Blade that week, and he was not interested in the second form of the Lin Blade. He asked me whether I could keep a secret from my father. I said yes. He said, Then keep this one from yourself, too."

The old man's voice has dropped. He is looking at the handprint, not at the boy.

"The hill is not ours," he says. "We only hold it."

The words hang in the warm air of the stair.

"I did not understand. I thought he meant the Compact, the sect's claim, the Hall's survey. He meant something else, and he died before he could say what. All I was left with was the key and the stair, and a rule that has never been broken: the Patriarch comes down once, at his appointment, and sees this. And then, until his own end, he stays away." A faint, wry curve touches his mouth. "I have broken that rule four times in the last month. I expect the stone has opinions."

"Did Zhao Heng's family ever come here?"

"Once. His grandfather, in the days when the Compact was still warm. Shoucheng walked him to the top of the stair, showed him the first ten steps and told him it was a cellar. The old man was no fool. He said nothing, and he went home, and on his deathbed he told a boy of nine named Heng that there was something under the Green Pine worth more than the spring." Grandfather's eyes finally come up. "Heng has spent a hundred and seventy years looking at my hill the way a man looks at a lock. He is only now strong enough to try the door."

He lets the Light Orb rise again to its ordinary glow. The lines vanish. The step becomes a plain dark stone.

"That is what is at the bottom of the stair, Jian. A handprint, and a sentence I do not understand. I wanted you to have seen it before tomorrow. In case there is no day after tomorrow for me to show you."

* * *

They sit on the thirty-ninth step, side by side, because Grandfather says his knees do not care for the fortieth.

The old man takes a flat leather flask from his sleeve and drinks. Jian does not ask what is in it. It smells of pine and plum wine. The Light Orb rests on the step between them, making a small gold room in the dark.

"I am going to say something," says Grandfather, "and you are not going to answer it."

"Yes, Grandfather."

"I will never ask you what you are."

Lin Jian does not move.

"I want that said, because you have been waiting for the question since spring, and it is not kind to make a person wait. I am not going to ask. I am too old, and I have too little time, and I find that I do not need to know." The flask clinks against his teeth. "But I am not blind. A patriarch who is not blind is a patriarch who has not been paying attention. So I will tell you what I have seen, and you may do with it what you like."

He raises one finger.

"A child of two, who looks at a fern as if it owes him an explanation. A child of four who corrects the cook's measures, politely, and is right." A second finger. "A child of six who asks Hu where the iron goes when it burns. A child of seven who takes my seal-hand letter and finds the one stroke I made badly in the winter of my fortieth year, and says so in front of the whole table." The third. "A child who is nine and has the Qi of a boy of thirteen, and the patience of a man of fifty, and who has not, in all that time, once asked me for anything for himself."

The old voice is very quiet.

"And last month, a child who stood in my chamber, over a pill that would have killed me, and said, in the calm voice of someone reading me the price of rice, Grandfather, I can fix this. And did."

Lin Jian's throat has closed. He looks at the toe of his boot.

"None of it is a crime. None of it is evil. I have looked, and I know evil; I have been at the Hall's table with the men who sell it by the pound. If you had been a thing that wished us harm, you would have been very much better at hiding it." Grandfather lowers his hand. "You were a child with a gift who wanted to be loved. That is what I saw. And I thought: whatever else this boy is, he is a Lin, and the Lins have never in six generations turned a child away from the door."

"I..." says Lin Jian, and cannot.

"Don't."

The old man puts the flask away. His hand, when it comes to rest on Jian's shoulder, is warm, and broad, and so thin that the bones lie along it like the ribs of a leaf.

"I only wanted to say," says Grandfather, "that if I live through tomorrow, I shall go on not asking. And if I do not, then you will know that this is what I thought, at the end, and that I thought it with a clear head and a glad heart."

For a while neither of them says anything.

Then, because he is nine years old and because there is nothing else that can be said, Lin Jian leans his head against the old green sleeve, and Grandfather lets him.

* * *

The key is in a plain wooden case, in a niche cut into the stair wall at the thirty-sixth step.

It is a disk of bronze the size of a child's palm, as thick as two coins, with a hole through the middle and a pine crest cast in relief on one face. On the other is a small square seal, scratched with a single line of small characters. It is old, and warm, and heavier than it looks.

"The Formation Key," says Grandfather. "It is the only one. It is tied to the anchor plate at the foot of the stairs, and through the plate to the twelve pins of the ring, the nine on the road, and the eighteen nails at the gate. Whoever holds it can lift the whole net and pull it tight, in any shape his mind can hold." A pause. "I have charged the plates every night for a month. They will hold what I have given them, and a little more. I have also done something I should not have, which is to ask the key to register a new name."

"Whose?"

"Yours."

The disk rests in his palm. The characters on the seal are old Lin script, and at the end of the line, in the fresh ink of a man's hand still wet from the brush, is Lin Jian.

"Not Wenyuan. Not Hu. Not Mao, who is the better fighter and the worse pupil. You." Grandfather's eyes are very steady. "I have watched you lay every pin and every nail with your own hands, and I have seen you do something with them that I could not do with forty years of practice. You think of the ring not as a wall but as a shape. Wenyuan builds a wall. He is good at it. You build a trap."

"I am nine."

"And you are the only person on this hill who can use it. Which one of those facts do you think matters more?"

Lin Jian folds his fingers over the bronze. It is warm. Under the warmth, faintly, there is a pulse.

```

Net state: idle, integrity 100%

CE: +3 (total: 137 / 400)
```

He stops reading at the third line.

Telemetry. The key does not merely command the net; the net speaks back through it. Every pin's load, every nail's strain, the Qi pouring through the anchor plate. It is a cable running into the middle of a building, and at the end of it, on the other side of the stone, a living man will be holding the plate with his bare palm for the next seven hours.

He thinks: I can watch him.

He does not say it. He has become very good at not saying things.

"The net has limits," says Grandfather, as if reading it off his face. "It will hold a late-stage Foundation Establishment cultivator for a quarter of an hour. Perhaps a little more, if the pins are fed and the nails are kept dry. A peak Foundation Establishment cultivator for half that. It will not hold Heng, if he wishes to cross it, for long. But he will not wish to cross it at once. He will wish to look at it, because he does not understand it. That is the quarter hour I am buying."

"Why only the Lins?"

"Because Shoucheng made it so." Grandfather lays the old sword across his knees. "No one goes down these steps who is not Lin. The key will answer only to blood, and the stair will answer only to the key. If Zhao Heng's men reach the top, they will find a stone floor and a door they cannot open. If he opens it by force, the key can fold the stair on top of him." He breathes out slowly. "I would prefer that it did not come to that. A man who dies at the bottom of a hole is the worst kind of martyr."

* * *

The rest of the night is for plans, and the plans are short.

"Tomorrow, at dawn, I enter the chamber and begin," says Grandfather. "You know the pill. Four stages. Absorption, one to two hours; the pill comes apart and the spirit of it flows into the marrow. Compression, four to seven, when the whole of my Qi is crushed into a single seed in the lower field. Foundation, the seed becomes the base. Stabilization, the base takes root. I have done three-quarters of it in my sleep for ten years." He smiles briefly. "It is the last quarter that tends to be fatal."

"What happens if you are interrupted?"

"In the first stage, a headache. In the third or fourth, a man's channels tear and he is a cripple. In the second..." He lifts a hand and lets it fall. "The seed explodes. In a Qi Refining ninth stage, that means a hole in the ground the size of a granary. In a man with a pill in him, it is rather worse."

"Then the ring..."

"The ring buys me time. The family buys the ring time. And you, my boy, are the one who sits on top of the stair with the key, and watches the plate, and tells me, if I am able to hear you, whether the roof is still on the house."

"Can you hear me?"

"I will be in the middle of the most important hour of my life, breathing in rhythm with the mountain." The old man's mouth quirks. "So, no. But I will feel the plate, if you pulse it. Three short, and then one long. It is the oldest Lin signal there is. It means stay."

Lin Jian repeats it. Three short, one long. It is not a word; it is a heartbeat.

"And the rest of them?"

Grandfather tells him. It takes some time, and he asks no questions, because there are none to ask. It is a plan that has been drawn and redrawn in the Patriarch's own head for a month, and he has looked at it from every side.

Old Hu at the main gate, with his rod and his cauldron-lid shield, because Hu does not care to be told where to stand and the gate is the one place on the hill where nobody tries. Uncle Mao and six of the cousins on the gate tower: Mao for the Earth Rampart, the cousins for the talismans, fire and ice and the Sound Mirage, anything that can be thrown from a height at a man on a horse. Mother on the tower beside them, with the Tidal Spear, because in all of Green Pine there is one person who can put a needle through a window at eighty paces. Wenyuan on the east wall, with the village guards and their thirty Silent Spears. Feng with the runners, wherever the line is thinnest. The children and the old in the granary cellar behind the Door-Sealing slip, with Aunt Meirong and Third Aunt's medicine chest.

"And the hut?" says Lin Jian.

"You."

"Alone?"

"You and the stone and the door." Grandfather looks at him. "If it all falls, it falls. And if it does, you are to take the key and go down, and close the stair behind you, and sit with the ring until it ends."

"That is not a plan, Grandfather. That is a funeral."

"Yes," says the old man comfortably. "It is. I find it clarifies the mind."

At the second hour past midnight, something warm touches the inside of Lin Jian's sleeve.

He freezes. It is a small warmth, like a coal laid on the skin. It comes again, once, twice. Then it is gone.

"Greater Boundary Alarm," Grandfather says. He has not turned his head. "You tethered one to your wrist before you came down?"

"Father's slip. The paired one. I put the other on the ridge."

"Then someone is on the ridge." The old man closes his eyes, the picture of repose. "Your cousin will deal with it. He is a good boy. He will use a spear, and Kai will throw something, and they will both be very pleased with themselves." A pause. "Don't go up."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were. It was in your shoulders." The eyes open. "Sit. We have a little while yet."

* * *

They climb the stair at five.

The upper steps are cold again. The light is gray at the top, the thin pale gray of a morning that has not yet decided to be a morning. Behind them, from the foot of the stair, comes a sound Lin Jian has not heard before, not a noise, exactly, but a settling, like a very large animal turning over in its sleep.

At the threshold of the stone hut, Grandfather stops.

He looks at Jian for a long moment. Then he lays his hand flat on the boy's head, as he did when Jian was three, and says nothing at all. He turns and goes back down into the dark, a tall straight figure in a deep-green robe, with the Light Orb swinging at his side.

Lin Jian watches him go until the stairs have swallowed him.

Then he steps out into the yard, with the bronze disk closed in his left fist and the door at his back, and pulls it shut.

A bar drops into place with a sound like the end of a sentence.

He remembers the next few minutes in pieces. Feng, grimy and bandaged, with a lantern. A quick, quiet conversation. The blue light of the ring coming up behind him, one pin at a time, and the cicadas going silent, and the smoke on the east ridge. Then the big bell, ringing across the valley, and he is walking, steadily and straight, to the kitchen.

* * *

"Eat," says Mother.

She has not asked where he has been. She is standing at the long kitchen table in her working short robe, with the Tidal Spear leaning in the corner and a small crowd of preoccupied relatives moving around her like water around a stone, and she has put a bowl of rice porridge in front of him with a spoon standing upright in it.

Old Nan has lit the stove with a pinch of Fire Starter, the old way, crumbling a little orange slip into the grate. The kettle is already steaming. Beside it, the water jug is filling by itself, drop by slow drop, from a small blue slip pasted inside the lid. Somebody in the corner is sharpening a Silent Spear, and somebody else has propped the kitchen door open with a bucket of Flame-Burst slips, and the whole room smells of rice and pepper-ink and pine smoke.

Lin Jian sits and picks up the spoon. He finds that his hand is not quite steady.

"Is it begun?" says Mother, very low.

"He went down at dawn."

"And you."

"I have the key." He shows her, briefly, then closes his fist again. "Father's slip woke me at two. Feng caught a scout."

"I know. He told me. He is very proud." She lays a hand flat on the table beside the bowl, not touching him. "You will be in the hut."

"Yes."

"Alone."

"Yes."

"Then I am going to say it once, and you will let me." She takes a breath. "I am not going to ask what you are doing, Jian. I did not ask in the spring, I did not ask at the council, and I will not ask now. I only want you to know what I would do, if I were you. I would eat. I would drink. And I would not look at the door."

"I can't promise that."

"Then promise the first two."

"I promise the first two."

"Good." The corner of her mouth moves. It is the closest to a smile he has seen in a month. "I will bring you water at nine. And at noon, if it's quiet, bread. And when it's over, one way or another..." She stops. Her eyes are very clear. "When it's over, you come and find me. Wherever I am. You do not wait for someone to send for you."

"I will."

"Say it."

"When it's over, I will come and find you."

She nods, once. She picks up the Tidal Spear. At the door, she turns, and for a moment the whole kitchen goes quiet around her, like a pond, and in the bright doorway her small figure is as straight as a spear.

"Eat," says Su Qinghe, and goes out.

He eats. All of it. The porridge is hot, and a little salty, and it is the best thing he has ever tasted.

* * *

By the time the sun is high enough to strike the stone hut's tiles, every soul on Green Pine Hill is at their place.

Lin Jian sees it from the narrow window of the hut, a slit no wider than his hand cut for Shoucheng's guard a hundred and fifty years ago. He has set a lamp on the floor and a cushion on the lid of a rice barrel and a bowl of water at his side. He sits on the cushion with his legs folded and his back against the wall. The bronze disk lies in his palm. Under his thumb, steady as a heartbeat, the ring thrums.

Through the slit, he sees the yard, the wall, the gate tower.

Old Hu is at the main gate, in a leather apron and an old padded cloak, a stout figure with his rod across his shoulders and a round iron lid strapped to his left arm. He is not looking at anyone. He is looking at the road. On the tower above him stand Uncle Mao, vast and calm, with both hands resting on his belt, and the cousins in a ragged row: Wenshi's boys with their Flame-Burst slips fanned in their fingers like playing cards, Qiao with her wind slips pinned in a crown in her hair. Mother is at the end of the line, a little apart, with the Tidal Spear held low and her eyes fixed on the horizon.

On the east wall, Father is in his gray cloak, with his left hand loose at his side and his sword at his hip. He has put on his old fighter's belt. Lin Jian has not seen him wear it in all his life. Along the parapet, the village guards stand in a long double rank, thirty men in bronze arm-guards with Silent Spears grounded, their faces tight and scrubbed and ordinary. Farmers, most of them. Their wives are somewhere behind the granary. They have been told to stay out of the way if it comes to it and to run if they must. Few of them will.

And in the middle of the yard, Feng stands with his eight runners, and the first light catches the edge of the practice sword.

Everyone, thinks Lin Jian. Every one of them. He holds the key tighter.

The numbers flow across the edge of his sight, lazy and regular. He reads them the way a night nurse reads a chart, with the whole of his attention and none of his heart.

Absorption. Fifty-two beats a minute. Steady. He lets his breath out. For the first hour he does nothing but watch the numbers go up, and listen to the stone.

At the end of the hour, the pill is gone.

Now it begins. He feels it through the key, through his palm, up his arm into his teeth: a low, slow, enormous pressure, like the bottom of the sea settling on the world. The cicadas have not made a sound since dawn. Even the birds are silent.

Mother comes at nine with the water. She sets the cup down at his elbow, on the barrel lid, and does not speak. She lays her palm for a moment on the top of his head and goes out. He drinks, and the telemetry tells him 51 percent, and the sun climbs the tiles and shifts across the floor.

At eleven the Qi in the plate is a drumbeat. At half past, it has the taste of copper. He can feel Grandfather now, as one feels someone else's pulse, a mountain of will pressed into a space no bigger than a fist, and the Light Orb on the floor flickers each time the pressure rises, as if the lamp itself were afraid.

Seventy-four. A little more than half the hour. Four more hours, and the seed will be set and the hardest part will be done.

At noon, a bell begins to ring on the north road.

It is not the big bell. It is the little one, the one the lookouts carry, struck three times, and again, and again, a thin, fast, silver sound. Triple bell. Riders on the road. He is on his feet before he knows he has moved, with one eye pressed to the slit.

They come out of the trees at the bottom of the hill in a long, dark column. Thirty of them, more, on tall horses, in gray-green cloaks with the Zhao ridge-and-sun badge stitched on the shoulder. The hooves are soft on the packed earth, and the dust rises in a slow, golden cloud. At the front rides a man on a gray horse, upright in the saddle, in a plain brown robe, with a jade ring on his right hand that catches the sun.

He is smiling.

The column halts at the foot of the gate, two hundred paces from the wall. The dust drifts. The horses stamp and blow. And the man on the gray horse raises his right hand, and the sound of the world goes out of the air.

Then the voice comes, clear, warm, genial, carried on a thread of Qi that goes into every ear on the hill at once, as if the speaker were standing at their shoulder.

"Brother Lin!" calls Zhao Heng. "I've come to offer my congratulations in advance!"
